title: Everyone has gone astray (Romans 1:18–3:20)
hook: Paul argues that Jew and Gentile alike have missed the mark

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul introduced himself to a church in Rome he had never met, and your line was not ashamed. Did you introduce yourself kindly to someone new? Day three hundred thirteen.

A group chat, late in the evening. Someone starts listing everything wrong with everybody else. The coworker who never refills the coffee. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven. Everyone piles on. Then one friend types a single line: you do that too. Silence. Paul does exactly this to his readers in Rome. Through the rest of his first chapter he describes a world that has turned away from God: greed, envy, gossip, cruelty, people who know better and don't care. It's easy to hear the listeners nodding. Yes. Them. And then he turns around and points at the one nodding. Today's word is the one he's building toward.
screen: `A LIST OF EVERYONE ELSE'S WRONGS.` → `THE LISTENERS NOD.` → `THEN PAUL TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the turn, in the King James Bible: "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself." Whoever you are. The finger that was pointing out now points back. Paul builds his case in two halves. First, the nations who never had the law of Moses. They still had creation, he says: God's power can be seen in the things that are made. And they still had a conscience, a law written on the heart, that sometimes accuses and sometimes excuses. Second, his own people, the Jewish people, who had the law and the promises. Paul is a Jew himself, arguing as an insider, and he says having the law is a gift, but hearing it isn't the same as keeping it. Then he lands the point with a string of lines, mostly from the Psalms: "There is none righteous, no, not one." Nobody gets to stand on the balcony and look down. Now the word. In Greek, the word Paul uses for sin is hamartia. Its verb, in older Greek, could mean to miss: a spear thrown that falls short of the target. So sin, for Paul, is not only a list of bad deeds. It's a condition everyone shares, a whole aim that's off. Christians describe how deep that goes in different ways, and we'll meet those differences in the days ahead. But the text is plain on one thing: Paul isn't sorting the world into good people and bad people. He's putting everyone in the same room. And that's where the good news can start.
screen: `WHOSOEVER THOU ART THAT JUDGEST.` · `CREATION AND CONSCIENCE.` · `THE LAW, HEARD AND NOT KEPT.` · `HAMARTIA: MISSING THE MARK.` · then, large: `THERE IS NONE RIGHTEOUS, NO, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one way you missed the mark. Settle, and breathe. Let yesterday play back slowly, like a video. Somewhere in it, you aimed at kindness, or patience, or honesty, and fell a little short. Don't hunt for the worst thing you've ever done. Just find one small, real miss. Name it plainly, without a speech in your own defense and without beating yourself up. Then notice: whoever you judged this week has missed too, and so have you. Same room. If you pray, you can bring that one miss to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Sin. Hamartia in Greek, a word that could mean missing the mark. For Paul, not just bad deeds but a condition everyone shares.
Your line: all of us. Today, the next time you catch yourself judging someone, finish the sentence honestly: and I do that too. Day three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Some Christians end the day with an examination of conscience: looking back over it, naming where they fell short, and asking God's forgiveness.

original.note: Greek: sin. its verb could mean to miss, as a thrown spear misses its target.

trapdoor: what you thought: sin is a list of bad things other people do.
what it means: Paul argues that everyone, with the law or without it, has fallen short. nobody stands above anyone else.
what a scholar hears: hamartia, from a verb that in Homer can describe a spear missing its target. Paul uses it for a power and a condition, not only for single deeds.

notes: The list of wrongs in Romans 1:18–32 includes 1:26–27, which churches read in different ways; the script summarizes the list generally and does not address those verses. Keeper may want to decide whether to mention them.

Hamartia as 'missing the mark': the verb hamartano is used in Homer for missing with a spear. The archery/target gloss is popular and sound for the root, but Paul's usage should not be reduced to it; the script says 'could mean'. Confirm.
Romans 2:14–15 (law written on the heart, conscience accusing or excusing) is paraphrased.
Care taken to present Paul as a Jew arguing as an insider, and to present Jewish possession of the law as a gift (Romans 3:1–2), to avoid anti-Jewish framing.
Romans 3:10–18 is a chain of quotations mainly from the Psalms; confirm the phrasing 'a string of lines from the Psalms' (Isaiah is also quoted in 3:15–17).
